## Overview

Overview

In this tutorial, we will use `{dplyr}` to practice core data-wrangling tasks in R. We will work with the penguins data from the `palmerpenguins` package.

By the end of the tutorial, you should be able to:

use `filter()` to keep observations that meet specified conditions;
use `select()` to keep or remove variables;
use `relocate()` to reorder variables without dropping columns;
use `rename()` and `rename_with()` to change variable names;
use `mutate()` to create or modify variables;
combine `group_by()` with `summarise()` to calculate summaries for groups; and
combine multiple `{dplyr}` functions with the pipe (`|>`) to build data-wrangling workflows.

::: callout-note
This lesson is an instructor-led adaptation inspired by Allison Horst's *Wrangling penguins: some basic data wrangling in R with dplyr* LearnR tutorial. The structure and explanations here have been rewritten for a classroom Quarto workflow, and current dplyr syntax is used where the package has changed.

Source: <https://allisonhorst.shinyapps.io/dplyr-learnr/>
:::

## Setup

You will need the `tidyverse`, `palmerpenguins`, and `nycflights13` packages.

```{r}
#| label: setup

options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

if (!requireNamespace("pak", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pak")
}

packages <- c("tidyverse", "palmerpenguins", "nycflights13")
missing_packages <- packages[
  !vapply(packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  pak::pak(missing_packages)
}

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(nycflights13)
```

The `tidyverse` is a collection of R packages designed for data science. **dplyr** is the tidyverse package focused on data manipulation.

Some common dplyr functions are:

| Function                     | Main purpose                               |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `filter()`                   | Keep rows that meet conditions             |
| `select()`                   | Keep or remove columns                     |
| `relocate()`                 | Move columns                               |
| `rename()`                   | Rename columns                             |
| `mutate()`                   | Create or modify columns                   |
| `group_by()` + `summarise()` | Calculate summaries by groups              |
| `across()`                   | Apply a function to multiple columns       |
| `count()`                    | Count observations by groups               |
| `case_when()`                | Create values based on multiple conditions |

## Meet the data

The `penguins` data contain measurements from three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins.

Take a first look at the data.

```{r}
penguins
```

```{r}
glimpse(penguins)
```

The data contain eight variables:

- `species`: penguin species
- `island`: island where the penguin was observed
- `bill_length_mm`: bill length in millimeters
- `bill_depth_mm`: bill depth in millimeters
- `flipper_length_mm`: flipper length in millimeters
- `body_mass_g`: body mass in grams
- `sex`: sex of the penguin
- `year`: study year

The data are already **tidy**: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value occupies one cell.

Let's look at the first 10 rows. 

Note we are not creating an object, so the result from the following code will print out immediately (and will not save or change the dataframe). Also remember the pipe `|>`, which is a cornerstone of data wrangling with the tidyverse.

```{r}
penguins |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

# `filter()`: keep rows

Use `filter()` when you want to keep observations that satisfy one or more conditions.

The general structure is:

``` r
data |>
  filter(condition)
```

## Filtering categorical variables

Keep only Chinstrap penguins. Note that we use `==` and not `=`. While you would normally assign the filtered dataframe to a new object (i.e., `penguins <- pengions |>...`) we will not do this so we can keep working with the same dataframe (or we'd have to rename the object something different each time).

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap")
```

To keep rows matching **either** of two categories, use `|` for OR.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap" | species == "Gentoo")
```

When checking several possible values of the same variable, `%in%` is often easier to read.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species %in% c("Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))
```

::: callout-warning
`species == c("Chinstrap", "Gentoo")` does **not** mean "Chinstrap or Gentoo." For that task, use `%in%`.
:::

## The pipe operator

The native R pipe, `|>`, can be read as **"and then."** We call this the native version because R did not used to have a native version and just had a `dplyr` version, `%>%`. If you ever see `%>%`, it is the same thing.

``` r
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap")
```

This means: start with `penguins`, **and then** filter the rows of observations with Chinstrap penguins.

## Combining conditions

Keep Adelie penguins observed on Dream Island. Note that here, we want both conditions and they are in different columns. You can do this by using a `,` (or `&`).

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Dream")
```

Again - a comma inside `filter()` means that **both** conditions must be true. You can also write the same logic with `&`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie" & island == "Dream")
```

## Filtering numeric variables

Lets go over the common comparison operators that you will often see and use:

| Operator | Meaning                  |
|----------|--------------------------|
| `==`     | equal to                 |
| `!=`     | not equal to             |
| `>`      | greater than             |
| `<`      | less than                |
| `>=`     | greater than or equal to |
| `<=`     | less than or equal to    |

You can use these within `filter()`. For example, keep penguins with flippers longer than 200 mm.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(flipper_length_mm > 200)
```

Keep penguins weighing 2900 g or less.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(body_mass_g <= 2900)
```

You can even combine categorical and numeric conditions. For example, keep penguins in the Adelie species that have a bill length of greater than 40 mm.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", bill_length_mm > 40)
```

## Excluding rows

Use `!=` when you want to keep rows that **do not** match a value. For example, the following keeps all penguin species with the exception of Chinstrap.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species != "Chinstrap")
```

# `select()`: keep or remove columns

Use `select()` to choose variables by name.

## Selecting individual columns

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(year, island, species)
```

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass_g)
```

The order of variables inside `select()` also controls their order in the output.

## Selecting a range of columns

Use `:` to select consecutive variables.This selects `species`, `body_mass_g`, and every column between them in the current column order.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(species:body_mass_g)
```

You can combine a range of columns with additional columns that you want to select.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(species:bill_depth_mm, year)
```

## Excluding columns

Use `-` to remove one column.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(-island)
```

Exclude a consecutive range.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(!(island:bill_depth_mm))
```

You can also use the `-`

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(-(island:bill_depth_mm))
```

Exclude several non-consecutive variables.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(!c(species, flipper_length_mm, year))
```

or, with the `-`:

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(-c(species, flipper_length_mm, year))
```

## Selection helpers

Selection helpers are useful when variable names follow patterns.

Select columns starting with `bill`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(starts_with("bill"))
```

Select columns ending with `mm`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(ends_with("mm"))
```

Select columns containing `length`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(contains("length"))
```

You can combine selection rules. The `|` operator selects columns that match either rule. This selects `bill_length_mm`, `bill_depth_mm`, and `flipper_length_mm`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(contains("length") | starts_with("bill"))
```

You can also use `&` to select columns that match both rules. This selects only `bill_length_mm`:

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(contains("length") & starts_with("bill"))
```

### Be careful with commas

A comma behaves differently inside `filter()` and `select()`.

In `filter()`, multiple conditions separated by commas are combined with AND:

```{r}
penguins |> filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Dream")
```

This is equivalent to:

```{r}
penguins |> filter(species == "Adelie" & island == "Dream")
```

Both keep penguins that are Adelie **AND** were observed on Dream Island.

In `select()`, however, a comma combines the columns returned by each selection:

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(contains("length"), starts_with("bill"))
```

This selects columns that match **either** rule: `bill_length_mm`, `flipper_length_mm`, and `bill_depth_mm`.

That is different from:

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(contains("length") & starts_with("bill"))
```

which selects only columns that match both rules: `bill_length_mm`.

So remember: in `filter()`, comma-separated conditions are combined with **AND**. In `select()`, comma-separated selections are combined together, like **OR**. In `select()`, `&` means a column must match **both** selection rules.

So `,` and `&` are interchangeable in `filter()`, but not in `select()`.

## Combining `filter()` and `select()`

Sometime you want to filter observations (rows), then variables (columns). For example, keep Gentoo penguins, then retain only island, sex, and body mass:

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>
  select(island, sex, body_mass_g)
```

Keep male penguins with flippers longer than 200 mm, then retain variables ending in `mm`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(sex == "male", flipper_length_mm > 200) |>
  select(ends_with("mm"))
```

You will get more practice with `select()` in the exercises portion of the class today.

# `relocate()`: move columns

`relocate()` changes column order without dropping variables.

If you provide only a variable name, that variable moves to the front. For example, `year` will now be the first column.

```{r}
penguins |>
  relocate(year)
```

Use `.after` to place a variable after another variable. Here, `flipper_length` will immediately follow `island`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  relocate(flipper_length_mm, .after = island)
```

Use `.before` to place a variable before another variable. `bill_length_mm` will come right before `year`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  relocate(bill_length_mm, .before = year)
```

You can also use selection helpers such as `where()`. The code below places all of the `numeric` columns after the columns that are `factors`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  relocate(where(is.numeric), .after = where(is.factor))
```

## Practice: `relocate()`

### Practice 1

Move `species` so that it appears immediately before `sex`.

```{r}

```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}

```

# `rename()`: rename columns

Use `rename()` to change variable names. The syntax is:

``` r
data |>
  rename(new_name = old_name)
```

Rename `island` to `palmer_island`.

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename(palmer_island = island)
```

Rename more than one variable at the same time.

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename(
    study_yr = year,
    mass = body_mass_g
  )
```

## `rename_with()`

`rename_with()` applies a function to selected column names.

Convert every column name to uppercase.

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename_with(toupper)
```

Convert only names ending in `mm` to uppercase.

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename_with(toupper, ends_with("mm"))
```

## Practice: `rename()`

### Practice 1

Convert the names of variables that begin with `bill` to uppercase.

```{r}
# Write your code here
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename_with(toupper, starts_with("bill"))
```
:::

# `mutate()`: create or modify columns

Use `mutate()` to add new variables or modify existing variables.

``` r
data |>
  mutate(new_variable = expression)
```

## Creating a new variable

Convert body mass from grams to kilograms.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)
```

Calculate the ratio of bill length to bill depth.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm)
```

## Creating several variables

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm,
    body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
    flipper_length_m = flipper_length_mm / 1000
  )
```

Create a sequential record number.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(record_number = row_number())
```

## Modifying an existing variable

If the name on the left side of `=` already exists, `mutate()` replaces that variable. The code below changes `island` to a character.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(island = as.character(island))
```

::: callout-warning
Overwriting a variable can be useful, but it also removes the original version. When learning or exploring, creating a new variable is often safer.
:::

`mutate()` can also call functions from other packages. For example, `forcats::fct_relevel()` changes the order of factor levels. You can check out the `forcats` package by running `?forcats` (or `??forcats` if the package is not installed.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    island = forcats::fct_relevel(
      island,
      "Torgersen", "Biscoe", "Dream"
    )
  )
```

## Practice: `mutate()`

### Practice 1

Create `year_fct`, containing `year` converted to a factor.

```{r}
# Write your code here
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
penguins |>

```
:::


# `group_by()` + `summarise()`: summaries by group

Often, you will want to summarize data so to find out certain things about your data. For the penguins example, we may want to know:

What is the mean body mass for each species?
How many penguins were observed on each island?
What is the mean flipper length for males and females within each species?

`group_by()` tells dplyr which groups should be treated separately. `summarise()` then calculates one or more summary statistics for each group.

Without grouping, `summarise()` returns an overall summary. If we run the code below, we get a mean mass for all penguins. But that is not very useful. 

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    mass_mean = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

With grouping, the same calculation is performed separately for each group.

## One summary by one group

Calculate mean body mass by species.

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mass_mean = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

`na.rm = TRUE` tells `mean()` to ignore missing values when calculating the mean.

## Multiple summaries

Calculate mean and standard deviation of body mass by species.

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mass_mean = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_sd = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

## Multiple grouping variables

Calculate mean and standard deviation of bill length for each species-by-sex combination.

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(
    bill_length_mean = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    bill_length_sd = sd(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The `.groups = "drop"` argument makes the returned table ungrouped after the summary is calculated. This is a good idea to do because after summarise(), you often want the resulting table to behave like a regular ungrouped data frame.

If grouping remains, later operations such as mutate(), filter(), or another summarise() may still be carried out separately within those groups, sometimes unintentionally.

## Combine wrangling steps

Here, we want to understand the minimum and maximum flipper length for male Adelie penguins on each island. We will need to use `filter`, `group_by`, and `summarise` to calculate the minimum and maximum flipper length by island for male Adelie penguins. First, we have to filter `species` by `Adelie`, `sex` by `male`. Then we have to `group_by` island. Last, we have to `summarise` the `flipper_length_mm` by its maximum and minimum value using the `max` and `min` functions.

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", sex == "male") |>
  group_by(island) |>
  summarise(
    flip_max_length = max(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    flip_min_length = min(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

## Practice: `group_by()` + `summarise()`

### Practice 1

For Chinstrap penguins, calculate minimum and maximum flipper length by island. Name the new variables `flip_min` and `flip_max`.

```{r}
# Write your code here
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap") |>
  group_by(island) |>
  summarise(
    flip_max = max(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    flip_min = min(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::

### Practice 2

What is the average bill length-to-depth ratio for each penguin species?

Hint: in one pipeline, you will need to:

1.  Create `bill_ratio` as bill length divided by bill depth.
2.  Keep only `species` and `bill_ratio`.
3.  Group by species.
4.  Calculate the mean bill ratio for each species and call it `bill_ratio_mean`.

```{r}
# Write your code here
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm) |>
  select(species, bill_ratio) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    bill_ratio_mean = mean(bill_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::

# Summary

The dplyr functions covered in this tutorial answer different types of data-wrangling questions:

| Question | Function |
|----|----|
| Which observations do I want? | `filter()` |
| Which variables do I want? | `select()` |
| Where should variables appear? | `relocate()` |
| What should variables be called? | `rename()` |
| What new variables do I need? | `mutate()` |
| What summaries do I need by group? | `group_by()` + `summarise()` |
| Can I repeat the same operation across variables? | `across()` |
| How many observations are in each group? | `count()` |
| Can I assign values based on several conditions? | `case_when()` |

The main idea is that these verbs can be chained together with `|>` to build a readable sequence of data-wrangling steps.
